Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for West Indies' reply with the bat. The New Zealand players are in a huddle, having a detailed chat with captain Amelia Kerr, pumping up her ladies. Now, they spread out to take their respective fielding spots. Qiana Joseph walks out with Hayley Matthews to open for the Windies. And it will be Rosemary Mair to open the attack for the Kiwis. Joseph to face. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Alleyne’s lethal spell - The bowling from the West Indies was highly disciplined for the most of the game, led by an exceptional performance from Alleyne. Alleyne was the undisputed standout performer as she single-handedly applied the brakes on NZ's scoring rate, striking three times in a span of just two overs to finish with magnificent figures of 4 for 27 from her four overs. Skipper Hayley Matthews chipped in with a wicket of her own to keep the pressure on. While the final target is not overly massive, the formidable bowling unit that the New Zealand side possesses means this will surely be a stiff challenge for the Windies if NZ can make early inroads into their top order.

A quick word with Isabella Gaze - Isabella Gaze says it felt good and that they wanted to attack upfront. About the total, she says they are happy with the runs they have manage to put on the board. On the wicket, she notes it's a great surface where the ball comes onto the bat nicely. On the score, she credits Maddy for playing well at the death and adds that the bowlers will need to keep attacking the stumps. She says she's really excited to get going, pointing out that the team has been there for a few weeks and is happy to finally get out on the field. On advice for the bowlers, she suggests mixing up the pace, since anything on the quicker side tends to come onto the bat nicely.

Flying catches and middle-order resilience - The West Indies maintained high intensity on the field, holding onto their catches remarkably well to stem the flow of runs. Devine was eventually sent packing in the 20s thanks to another piece of fielding brilliance, which saw Claxton take a spectacular diving catch to break the dangerous stand. Halliday then joined forces with Maddy Green to add a valuable 35 runs for the fifth wicket, with Halliday top-scoring for her side by fighting hard into the 40s. Even though Green, Devine, and Gaze all batted well for their respective contributions, the regular fall of wickets continuously bothered the New Zealand side, leaving them feeling a few runs short of where they could have finished.

Blazing start followed by a sudden slump - New Zealand Women finish their 20 overs with a score of 162 on the board and will be reasonably happy with the competitive total they have posted. The White Ferns started the contest in an attacking manner, with Izzy Gaze smashing the absolute majority of the runs in a flying opening partnership that added 49 runs in just 5.5 overs. However, the West Indies quickly fought back to trigger a collapse, reducing New Zealand from a comfortable 49 for no loss to a shaky 56 for 3. With the batting side in a bit of disarray, skipper Sophie Devine was joined by Brooke Halliday, and the duo expertly stabilized the innings by adding 45 crucial runs for the fourth-wicket partnership.

Good awareness and running! New Zealand Women finish at 162/6. A slower one at 89.5 kph, on a length and outside the off stump. The stand between Devine and Halliday was brewing nicely, but the captain herself put her hand up to push them for another rebuild. The run rate is not that threatening, but the Kiwis will need to score in excess of 160 or 170 to post a challenging total. The Windies have managed to squeeze in many dot balls and have slowed down the scoring considerably. Commentary.Commentary: Right. God Defend New Zealand and Rally 'Round the West Indies are proudly sung in the middle with high emotions dripping in both camps. It is now time to get Match 4 underway in Southampton. The players of West Indies form a huddle near the ropes before scattering out. Out walk the two Kiwi openers - Georgia Plimmer and Isabella Gaze. The Women in Maroon are going with spin straightaway. Zaida James will bowl the first over. She bowls slow left-arm. No slip in place. Gaze to face. Here we go...

Time for the national anthems - The giant flags of both nations are unfurled in the middle. Out walk the match officials along with the match referee. Now, both captains lead their respective groups and get lined up in front of their respective flags. It will be New Zealand's first, followed by the cricket anthem of West Indies.

Jess Kerr, New Zealand Women, is up next - Jess says that they will look to attack from the start, and they can compete against any side in the world. She adds that she is working on her batting, and she wants to show up on the big stage. She reckons that they have learned a lot from their previous series against England and ends by saying that it has been great to play here.

Deandra Dottin, West Indies Women, is up for a chat - Dottin says that it gives a lot of confidence to them when they come to play the World Cup. She says that there are a lot of expectations from them and there were a lot of ups and downs till now, but they are in a good place now. She ends by saying that they have been training a lot and the warm-up games have helped them as well.

PITCH REPORT - Ian Smith and Tash Farrant are pitchside. They note that the boundary dimensions measure 65 and 63 metres to the square boundaries, 72 metres straight down the ground, and a shorter 55 to 56 metres into the corners, which allows batters to cleverly use the pace of the ball to their advantage. Mentions that this match takes place on pitch 10, a hybrid wicket that the head groundsman designed to offer enhanced pace, extra bounce, and more carry. Reckons that despite featuring some nice live grass, the surface is absolutely rock solid, leading the duo to predict that batters will thoroughly enjoy the conditions on a day heavily stacked in their favour. They add that any assistance for the seamers will occur strictly upfront, as the venue historically offers a little bit of swing in the air during the initial overs.

The skipper of New Zealand Women - Amelia Kerr says that they were looking to bat, so it's a good result for them. She says that it is good to see the crowd and the excellent support they have received so far. She reckons that they are getting used to the conditions. Ends by saying that Suzie Bates, Lea Tahuhu, Polly Inglis, and Flora Devonshire are not in the side.

The captain of West Indies Women - Hayley Matthews says that they will bowl first. She adds that they gave their youngsters a chance in the warmups, and they are ready for today. She adds that Taylor and Chinelle Henry have not recovered yet, and that's a big loss, but some youngsters come in for them. She reckons that it is good to see the youngsters get a chance and ends by saying that they are ready for today.

West Indies Women (Playing XI) - Qiana Joseph, Hayley Matthews (C), Shemaine Campbelle (WK), Deandra Dottin, Jahzara Claxton, Jannillea Glasgow, Aaliyah Alleyne, Zaida James, Shawnisha Hector, Afy Fletcher, Karishma Ramharack.
New Zealand Women (Playing XI) - Georgia Plimmer, Isabella Gaze (WK), Amelia Kerr (C), Sophie Devine, Brooke Halliday, Maddy Green, Izzy Sharp, Jess Kerr, Nensi Patel, Rosemary Mair, Bree Illing.
TOSS - Hayley Matthews, the skipper of West Indies Women, has won the coin flip and she has elected to BOWL first.

A grudge match - This is a direct rematch of the last World Cup semi-final, where New Zealand narrowly edged past the Windies before lifting the title. Today, all eyes will be on the blockbuster battle between the world's two finest all-rounders, Amelia Kerr and Hayley Matthews. Whoever wins that personal duel likely wins the match.  So, which side will come out on top? We shall find out. Toss and team news in a bit...

Caribbean powerhouses are ready to strike - On the other side, the West Indies are chasing the magic that made them world champions back in 2016. Captain Hayley Matthews and Qiana Joseph form a dangerous opening pair, with veterans Stafanie Taylor and the destructive Deandra Dottin holding down a scary middle order. They will need to shake off two warm-up losses and bounce back fast, especially with key all-rounder Chinelle Henry likely sidelined with an injury.

The White Ferns' last dance - New Zealand arrive with the trophy in hand but plenty of emotion in their hearts. This tournament marks the final international run for three Kiwi stalwarts. Suzie Bates, Sophie Devine, and Lea Tahuhu, who will all retire after this World Cup. Led by all-round superstar Amelia Kerr, the White Ferns look in good touch after winning both their warm-up games. Expect Bates and Izzy Gaze to set an aggressive tone right from the first ball.

Welcome to Southampton! Hello cricket fans, and welcome to a massive clash at Southampton as the ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 kicks off for Group B. The defending champions, New Zealand, are taking on the explosive West Indies. With tournament hosts and favorites England waiting in this tough group, a winning start today is absolutely crucial for both sides to eye that semi-final spot.
... MATCH DAY ...

Reigning champions take center stage - The early stages of a global tournament often carry a unique blend of excitement and anxiety, and Match 4 of the ICC Women’s T20 World Cup 2026 promises exactly that as West Indies Women lock horns with New Zealand Women. In a tournament where momentum can shift rapidly and a single poor outing can complicate qualification hopes, both teams arrive knowing the importance of making a statement early. While New Zealand begin the contest with the tag of slight favourites as the current champions and having an overall stable lineup, West Indies possess the sort of explosive, match-winning power that can turn games on their head within a matter of overs. Windies have the firepower - For West Indies Women, tournament cricket has often been a story of unpredictability. At their best, they are fearless, dynamic, and capable of dismantling even the strongest opposition with aggressive batting and athletic cricket. Yet consistency has remained their greatest challenge. Their fortunes frequently depend on whether their star names fire collectively, because when the Caribbean side gains momentum, they become one of the most dangerous T20 units in world cricket. The concern, however, lies in their tendency to suffer collapses when early wickets fall or when their bowling loses discipline under pressure. The spotlight for West Indies Women naturally falls on their experienced match-winners, namely skipper Hayley Matthews and the two veterans - Deandra Dottin and Stafanie Taylor. If West Indies are to challenge seriously, they need their all-rounders, particularly Chinelle Henry, to influence multiple phases of the contest rather than depending on isolated brilliance. The pressure of defending champions - New Zealand Women, on the other hand, enter this contest with a reputation for balance and structure. Historically, they have been a well-drilled tournament side, and the only side to break the duopoly of Australia and England in both T20 and ODI World Cups. Their strength lies in adaptability, whether defending totals or chasing under pressure, the White Ferns generally possess enough batting depth and bowling flexibility to stay in contests for longer periods. In tournament settings, that stability becomes invaluable, particularly in opening fixtures where nerves can influence decision-making. New Zealand's ability with the ball to squeeze scoring through disciplined lines and subtle changes in pace makes them particularly effective in T20 cricket. Against a side like West Indies, whose hitters thrive on rhythm, cutters and pace-off deliveries may prove especially valuable. However, just like West Indies, their star all-rounder and skipper, Amelia Kerr, will be key. She has probably been the most in-form women's cricketer in recent months and the hero of the 2024 Final will be hungry for more silverware. What about the playing conditions? With conditions expected to be dry in Southampton during the game, spin could play a defining role depending on surface conditions. West Indies have historically benefitted from spin-friendly tracks where their slower bowlers can control scoring rates and force risky shots. However, New Zealand’s batting line-up is often technically better equipped to negotiate spin through smart rotation of strike. That ability to deny dot-ball pressure could tilt the middle overs heavily in their favour. Predictions? On paper, New Zealand Women appear the more balanced and tactically secure side entering this fixture. Their batting depth, disciplined bowling attack, and superior fielding standards provide them with multiple avenues to control the contest. However, West Indies Women possess greater unpredictability and explosive potential, making them extremely dangerous if conditions suit aggressive strokeplay. Who are you backing for the win?
